overview: Engineering is this package's clearest counter-example to Medicine. Where Medicine runs through a structurally different mechanism from that country's own general admissions model in 13 of 15 countries, Engineering inverts the ratio: it is structurally different in only 5 of 15 (United States, United Kingdom, Canada, France, Germany); numerically stricter only -- same mechanism, higher bar -- in 7 of 15 (Italy, Spain, Ireland, Australia, New Zealand, Hong Kong, Turkey); and functionally indistinguishable from general admission in 3 of 15 (Netherlands, Switzerland, Singapore), a category Medicine never lands in anywhere in this package. Where Engineering is structurally different, the additions cluster into two kinds: a dedicated admissions-test layer absent from general admission (the UK's ESAT, successor to the discontinued ENGAA/PAT; Germany's TUM-confirmed Eignungsfeststellungsverfahren, real but not universal within Germany), and a separate application/decision layer organizationally distinct from the general admissions track at the same institution (the US's recurring school-within-university pattern at Cornell/Berkeley/Michigan; Canada's matching pattern at Waterloo and University of Toronto; and France's genuinely dual pathway -- CPGE-to-Grande-Ecole concours versus direct post-bac entry via Geipi Polytech/Puissance Alpha -- the sharpest single finding in this document). The 3 same-as-general-admission countries are confirmed, sourced absences, not under-research: Singapore's own NUS admission table shows every one of ten core Engineering majors requires no test or interview, while Architecture, Landscape Architecture and Industrial Design in the identical college all require one.

countries.scope: programme/track (two organizationally distinct selective mechanisms, neither run by an individual university's own admissions office, neither part of ordinary Licence admission)
countries.description: Two genuinely distinct pathways lead to the identical CTI (Commission des Titres d'Ingenieur)-accredited Diplome d'Ingenieur, confirmed via CTI's own accreditation framework treating both as equally valid. Pathway 1: CPGE (2-year classe preparatoire) entry is an ordinary Parcoursup dossier-reviewed voeu, not capacity-limited the way PASS/LAS is; the actual competitive event is a 'concours' roughly two years later, run entirely outside Parcoursup by inter-school exam-bank consortia -- X-ENS (Polytechnique/ENS/ESPCI), Centrale-Supelec (~3,577 places), Mines-Ponts/Mines-Telecom (1,569 + 2,237 places), CCINP/e3a-Polytech (~4,000 + 2,300+ places) -- written papers in April 2026, results in July 2026. Pathway 2: a continuous 5-year programme entered directly from Terminale via Parcoursup, with selectivity executed immediately by a dedicated concours network's own jury -- Geipi Polytech (35 public CTI-accredited schools; 3,997 general-Bac places + 245 technological-Bac places for 2026; general-Bac candidates sit a mandatory 3-hour written test, technological-Bac candidates instead undergo dossier review plus a motivation interview with no written test) and Puissance Alpha (19 major CTI-accredited schools across 35+ campuses; dossier review then a written exam, with top-ranked candidates sometimes exempted from the written stage). Selecting a concours network is one Parcoursup voeu regardless of member-school count; the deciding evaluation is the network's own jury, which feeds its ranking back into Parcoursup for the offer. CPGE-track selectivity is deferred two years and fully outside Parcoursup; post-bac-track selectivity is immediate and nominally routed through Parcoursup but decided by a multi-school jury, not any individual university's admissions office. Neither Geipi Polytech, Puissance Alpha, nor the CPGE concours-bank names appear anywhere in this package's existing france.md -- this is new territory added this pass.
countries.eligibility_determinants: For CPGE entry: Parcoursup dossier (livret scolaire, Fiche Avenir) exactly as for any other selective Parcoursup voeu. For the later concours: performance on that exam bank's own written and oral papers, roughly two years after CPGE entry. For post-bac direct entry: Parcoursup dossier plus, depending on Bac track and network, a written test (Geipi Polytech general-Bac; Puissance Alpha) or a dossier-plus-interview process (Geipi Polytech technological-Bac).
countries.strengthens_application: For the CPGE route, sustained performance across the full two years of preparatoire, since the concours tests accumulated preparation, not a single admissions file. For the post-bac route, strong terminale mathematics/physics-chemistry performance feeding both the Parcoursup dossier and (for general-Bac Geipi Polytech candidates) direct test performance; for technological-Bac candidates, a substantive motivation interview performance since no written test exists for that track.
countries.largely_irrelevant: General extracurricular breadth: no essay or recommendation-letter mechanism was found in either pathway's official materials reviewed this pass, consistent with the country doc's general finding that these are largely absent from French Licence-level admission.
countries.never_infer: Never present the CPGE-to-concours pathway and the post-bac direct-entry pathway as the same thing, or one as a lesser/fallback version of the other -- they are organizationally and temporally distinct routes to an identically CTI-accredited credential. Never assume entry into a CPGE class is itself the competitive event for engineering-school admission -- the concours two years later is. Never assume a DAP-track (foreign-diploma) applicant can access Geipi Polytech or Puissance Alpha without independent confirmation -- neither network's public materials confirmed this either way this pass, a genuine gap.
sources: docs/research/admissions-systems/france.md (Restricted / selective programmes, Admissions decision model sections)

countries.scope: programme, via a shared multi-university consortium instrument (ESAT) not run by any single university alone
countries.description: General UK admission runs on predicted-then-confirmed grades against a UCAS conditional offer, one shared personal statement, one shared reference, and rarely an interview outside Oxbridge. Engineering adds a real instrument absent from that baseline. ENGAA is confirmed discontinued (Cambridge Engineering moved away from it starting with 2024 entry) and replaced by the ESAT (Engineering and Science Admissions Test) -- confirmed directly, for the 2026-27/2027-entry cycle, as mandatory at Cambridge ('you must register in advance for this test'), Oxford Engineering Science (A*A*A with required A*s in Mathematics/Physics/Further Mathematics, ESAT 'required for everyone hoping to study Engineering Science'), Imperial College London, and UCL (BEng/MEng Electronic & Electrical Engineering from September 2027 entry) -- a shared consortium instrument, not a single university's bespoke test. TMUA does not extend to Engineering -- it remains scoped to Mathematics/CS/Economics/Statistics-adjacent courses, a different instrument for a different subject cluster. Where interviews exist (Cambridge, and Oxford for shortlisted candidates), they are subject-focused: Cambridge Engineering candidates commonly sit two interviews, one on mathematics/mathematical modelling and one on applied physics/mechanics, each roughly 25-40 minutes, built around unseen problems worked through in real time.
countries.eligibility_determinants: A*A*A/equivalent with required top grades in Mathematics/Physics/Further Mathematics (Oxford's stated bar); a registered, sat ESAT score ahead of the general UCAS deadline (October sitting mandatory for Oxbridge applicants); performance in subject-focused interview(s) where shortlisted.
countries.strengthens_application: Strong ESAT preparation and performance specifically -- the highest-leverage lever found this pass, mirroring UCAT's role for UK Medicine but for a different subject-matter test. Demonstrated ability to reason through unseen mathematics/physics problems live, the specific skill Cambridge's interview format is built to surface.
countries.largely_irrelevant: General extracurricular breadth beyond subject-adjacent ('super-curricular') engagement, consistent with the UK's general pattern already documented in the country doc; the personal statement's 'what else you've done to prepare' question rewards subject-relevant depth, not breadth.
countries.never_infer: Never assume ENGAA is still current -- it is discontinued. Never treat ESAT and TMUA as interchangeable or as variants of one test -- they serve different subject clusters and a student preparing the wrong one loses real time. Never assume ESAT is Cambridge/Oxford-exclusive -- Imperial and UCL also require it for specific programmes, and the exact list of ESAT-requiring universities/programmes should be re-checked per cycle.

countries.scope: university (confirmed at TU Munich for specific Bachelor's programmes; not national, and not universal even among technical universities)
countries.description: Engineering (Maschinenbau, Elektrotechnik, and related fields) is not one of hochschulstart's four nationally-coordinated NC subjects (Medicine, Dentistry, Veterinary Medicine, Pharmacy), ruling out a national-quota-style difference. A real university-level addition exists at some technical universities: confirmed directly this pass, TU Munich's Bachelor of Science in Mechanical Engineering (Maschinenwesen) runs through its own Eignungsfeststellungsverfahren (aptitude assessment procedure) rather than a plain Abiturnote threshold -- built around a mandatory written statement (German, up to two pages) giving reasons for choosing the programme and TUM specifically, explicitly framed as the basis for a possible follow-up interview; the process runs mid-July through September, after the general 15 July Wintersemester deadline. The same instrument governs several other TUM Bachelor's programmes (Informatik, Wirtschaftsinformatik, Management & Technology) -- a TUM-level selection instrument applied to a competitive-programme cluster, not invented for Engineering uniquely, but a genuine departure from the country doc's 'essays and interviews are not standard' finding. This is not universal: RWTH Aachen's own core Maschinenbau Bachelor's is currently (WS 2026/27) zulassungsfrei -- open admission, no selection procedure beyond eligibility -- though it was zulassungsbeschraenkt as recently as WS 2017/18, confirming an individual programme's mechanism can change over time. RWTH's own mandatory subject self-assessment ('Selbsttest') functions as a non-selective, informational completion requirement for enrollment, not a competitive filter.
countries.eligibility_determinants: At TUM-Eignungsfeststellungsverfahren-governed programmes: a formally correct application plus the written motivation statement, escalating to interview at the assessor's discretion. At zulassungsfrei programmes (e.g. RWTH Aachen Maschinenbau currently): the general HZB/Abitur-equivalence eligibility bar only, no selection at all.
countries.strengthens_application: At Eignungsfeststellungsverfahren-governed programmes, a substantive, specific written statement of motivation -- generic enthusiasm is unlikely to satisfy a process built to distinguish applicants beyond grades. At zulassungsfrei programmes, nothing beyond meeting the eligibility bar itself, since no selection or ranking occurs.
countries.largely_irrelevant: Essays/interviews at zulassungsfrei Engineering programmes -- there is no mechanism to receive them. General extracurricular activity outside the specific TUM-style written statement's own prompts.
countries.never_infer: Never assume one German technical university's Engineering admission mechanism generalizes to another -- TUM's Eignungsfeststellungsverfahren and RWTH Aachen's zulassungsfrei Maschinenbau are both real, confirmed, and different. Never assume a programme's current zulassungsfrei/zulassungsbeschraenkt status is stable over time -- RWTH's own Maschinenbau moved from restricted to open within roughly the last decade.
sources: docs/research/admissions-systems/germany.md (Restricted / selective programmes, Interviews / tests / portfolios sections)

countries.scope: university (a recurring pattern at specific universities, not a national rule; shape varies by institution)
countries.description: At a recurring set of major universities, applying to Engineering means applying to a named College/School of Engineering directly, with its own supplemental essays and sometimes a binding major choice, distinct from that same university's general liberal-arts admissions track. Confirmed directly this pass at three universities on two platforms: Cornell (via Common App -- an applicant selects one Cornell college and answers only that college's prompts; the College of Engineering requires six essays, including a 'why engineering' prompt up to 200 words plus four shorter responses on activities, awards, and intended contribution); UC Berkeley (via UC's own separate application, not Common App -- admission is directly by college and major, at least one of four required UC essays must address 'Why Engineering,' the major choice is binding at admission, and internal transfer from Letters & Science into Engineering after enrollment is confirmed difficult); and University of Michigan (via Common App -- Engineering is one of seven separate freshman-admitting schools/colleges, each requiring its own 100-550-word supplemental essay on institutional fit). Continuous with, not separate from, the country doc's existing finding that NYU Stern, Michigan Ross, and Cornell Dyson (business) are similarly named direct-admit schools -- Engineering is one of the recurring fields where this layer appears.
countries.eligibility_determinants: Whatever the host university's general eligibility bar is, plus a completed college-specific supplemental application (essays, sometimes a stated major commitment) submitted alongside, not instead of, the general application.
countries.strengthens_application: A focused, Engineering-specific essay response -- genuine reasons for choosing Engineering, concrete evidence of preparation or relevant experience, a clear sense of intended contribution to that college's community -- evaluated separately from the general application's own essay content, not a duplicate of it.
countries.largely_irrelevant: A strong general-application essay alone does not substitute for the college-specific supplement where one is required -- the two are evaluated as distinct artifacts.
countries.never_infer: Never assume every US university requiring Engineering applicants to name a major also makes that choice binding -- Berkeley's internal-transfer-difficulty finding does not automatically generalize to Cornell or Michigan without separate confirmation. Never assume MIT's direct-application, no-Common-App model (already documented at the country level) means every university with a College of Engineering works the same way -- the platform, the essay count, and the bindingness of the major choice all vary by institution.

countries.scope: university (confirmed at Waterloo and University of Toronto; UBC's equivalent extra-evidence layer is university-wide, not Engineering-triggered)
countries.description: Confirmed directly this pass, resolving the Waterloo lead: the Admission Information Form (AIF) is not Engineering-exclusive -- it is mandatory at Waterloo for all Engineering programmes (excluding Architecture), all Faculty of Mathematics programmes, and Computing and Financial Management, but explicitly not required for Waterloo's Arts, Environment, Health, or Science admissions. Within that scope it is substantive: five short-answer questions (a passion/strong interest and how it's been pursued; community involvement including any leadership role; a prompt asking the applicant to reflect on experiencing or witnessing unfair treatment; the applicant's primary goal for attending Waterloo; and outside-of-studies activities logged with hours in a chart), each capped at 150 words except the activities chart. The pattern recurs at University of Toronto via a different mechanism: U of T Engineering requires its own Online Student Profile (OSP) plus written AND timed-video Personal Profile Questions -- a layer U of T's own general Arts & Science admission (transcript-only, no required essay) does not have. UBC Engineering, by contrast, uses the same university-wide mandatory Personal Profile that applies to nearly every UBC programme, atop Grade-12 Math/Physics/Chemistry subject prerequisites -- the extra layer exists at UBC too, but is not what makes Engineering distinctive there.
countries.eligibility_determinants: The host university's general admission-average/subject-prerequisite bar, plus (at Waterloo and U of T specifically) a completed, separately-evaluated supplementary form (AIF, or OSP-plus-video Personal Profile Questions) submitted alongside the general application.
countries.strengthens_application: At Waterloo, breadth as much as depth -- the AIF's own guidance states the committee is 'not only looking for engineering-related extracurriculars.' At U of T, strong performance in both the written and video-response components of the Personal Profile, which the university frames as a holistic assessment of character, motivation, and fit.
countries.largely_irrelevant: At UBC, no Engineering-specific extra lever exists beyond the university-wide Personal Profile every applicant already submits -- there is no additional Engineering-only instrument to strengthen against.
countries.never_infer: Never assume a Canadian university's supplementary-application practice for Engineering generalizes to another Canadian university, or to a different faculty at the same one -- Waterloo's own AIF explicitly excludes Arts/Environment/Health/Science. Never assume Waterloo's AIF is unique to Waterloo -- it is not, though its specific form (five short answers) is Waterloo's own and differs from U of T's OSP-plus-video mechanism.

countries.scope: programme (most Engineering Bachelor's are open/threshold; specific popular programmes fall into the country's existing numerus fixus bucket)
countries.description: Most Dutch Engineering Bachelor's programmes are not numerus fixus: a Natuur & Techniek (N&T) VWO profiel (or the equivalent foreign-curriculum subject mapping) plus subject prerequisites establishes eligibility, with no ranking -- identical to the general threshold-based Dutch model already documented in this package, not something Engineering does differently. The exception is real but programme-level, not field-level: TU Delft's Computer Science & Engineering (CSE) is numerus fixus and uses a mandatory Mathematics + Systematic Reasoning test to stratify applicants into ranked bands before a hybrid lottery-within-band draw; TU Delft's Aerospace Engineering is separately numerus fixus (440 places confirmed for 2026-27) with its own decentralized selection procedure; by contrast TU Delft's own Werktuigbouwkunde (Mechanical Engineering) was confirmed this pass as carrying no numerus fixus. This is the Netherlands' own general numerus-fixus/open bifurcation (already documented for Medicine, Psychology, and others) showing up in specific popular Engineering programmes -- Engineering is not doing anything the Dutch system doesn't already do elsewhere.
countries.eligibility_determinants: At open programmes: VWO N&T profiel or equivalent subject mapping, no ranking. At the confirmed numerus fixus exceptions (TU Delft CSE, TU Delft Aerospace Engineering): the same eligibility bar plus a competitive selection step (Mathematics + Systematic Reasoning test and banded lottery for CSE; a separate decentralized procedure for Aerospace Engineering).
countries.strengthens_application: At open Engineering programmes, nothing beyond meeting subject prerequisites, since no ranking occurs. At TU Delft CSE specifically, strong performance on the Mathematics + Systematic Reasoning test.
countries.largely_irrelevant: Motivation letters/CVs at open (non-numerus-fixus) Engineering programmes -- not a requirement or a factor, matching the general Dutch open-programme pattern.
countries.never_infer: Never describe 'Dutch Engineering admission' as uniformly open or uniformly numerus fixus -- the correct unit is the individual programme, confirmed by the direct contrast between TU Delft's own CSE/Aerospace Engineering (numerus fixus) and Werktuigbouwkunde (open) in the same faculty at the same university.

countries.scope: university (ETH Zurich's general foreign-qualification framework, applied to Engineering exactly as to other non-Medicine fields)
countries.description: Confirmed directly this pass: ETH Zurich's Bachelor's programmes in Engineering (illustrated via Mechanical Engineering) use the same general ETH-wide foreign-qualification framework already documented in the country doc for Architecture and for foreign qualifications generally -- a Swiss Matura or an automatically-recognized foreign diploma meeting the direct-admission bar admits on a threshold basis, exam-free; a diploma falling short instead requires ETH's own Comprehensive or Reduced Entrance Examination (mathematics, physics, chemistry, biology). This is the general ETH mechanism for any field where the diploma isn't automatically recognized, not a dedicated Engineering instrument, and categorically different from EMS (used for Medicine/Dentistry/Veterinary Medicine/Chiropractic at most of the same institutions). No EMS-equivalent, Engineering-specific test or interview was found for ETH Zurich.
countries.eligibility_determinants: Swiss Matura, or a foreign diploma meeting ETH's automatic-recognition bar (exam-free), or a passed Comprehensive/Reduced Entrance Examination for a diploma that does not meet that bar -- the same determinants that apply to most non-Medicine ETH Bachelor's fields.
countries.strengthens_application: For applicants requiring the entrance examination, preparation in mathematics, physics, and chemistry specifically, since these are the tested subjects -- the same preparation that would strengthen an application to most other ETH science/technical fields, not an Engineering-specific lever.
countries.largely_irrelevant: Health-related or Medicine-adjacent experience, EMS-style aptitude scores -- these belong to a categorically different Swiss selection mechanism that does not apply to Engineering at all.
countries.never_infer: Never assume Switzerland's EMS mechanism (Medicine/Dentistry/Vet Med/Chiropractic) extends to Engineering in any form -- it does not. Never assume ETH's entrance-examination requirement is Engineering-specific -- it applies identically to any field a non-automatically-recognized foreign diploma holder wants to enter at ETH.
sources: docs/research/admissions-systems/switzerland.md (Subject prerequisites, Standardized tests, Restricted / selective programmes sections)

countries.scope: programme, confirmed field-by-field via NUS's own published admission-requirements table; ordinary major vs. elite honours sub-track split confirmed independently at NTU
countries.description: Confirmed directly this pass from NUS College of Design and Engineering's own official admission-requirements table: of the ten core Engineering majors listed (Biomedical, Chemical, Civil, Computer, Electrical, Engineering Science, Environmental, Industrial & Systems, Infrastructure & Project Management, Materials Science, and Mechanical Engineering), every single one shows 'Test or Interview: No.' Admission runs purely on the subject-prerequisite gate (H2 Mathematics/Further Mathematics, plus for some majors one of H2 Physics/Chemistry/Computing, or the IB/NUS High/polytechnic-diploma equivalent) feeding into NUS's ordinary open-competition academic review -- the same default mechanism the country doc documents for NUS generally. The same published table shows Architecture and Landscape Architecture both 'Test or Interview: Yes,' as does Industrial Design -- majors in the identical college. NUS's own elite sub-tracks (Engineering Scholars, Engineering and Medicine Track) also show 'Yes,' confirming that where an interview appears inside Engineering at NUS, it is scoped to a specific honours sub-programme, not the ordinary major. The same pattern recurs at NTU: its Renaissance Engineering Programme, a premier scholar track, has used a Multiple Mini Interview format since 2016, while ordinary NTU College of Engineering admission carries no confirmed general interview requirement. HKUST's School of Engineering (Hong Kong) states explicitly that interview is not a requirement for the School of Engineering, confirming the same pattern in a third system.
countries.eligibility_determinants: H2 Mathematics or Further Mathematics (A-Level track) or the equivalent IB/NUS High/polytechnic-diploma requirement, plus for several majors one further science/computing subject -- purely academic, no test or interview component for any of the ten core majors confirmed.
countries.strengthens_application: Academic performance in the relevant prerequisite subjects and standing within NUS's open-competition UAS ranking -- the same levers that strengthen any ordinary NUS application, since Engineering does not add its own evaluated component.
countries.largely_irrelevant: Portfolio material, interview preparation, or non-academic achievement lists specifically aimed at an Engineering admissions gate -- no such gate exists for the ten core majors confirmed; these levers matter for Architecture/Industrial Design/Landscape Architecture in the same college, or for Engineering's own elite honours sub-tracks, but not for ordinary Engineering admission.
countries.never_infer: Never assume Singapore's Medicine/Dentistry/Law/Architecture findings (ranking-position gates, mandatory tests, portfolio/interview requirements) extend to ordinary Engineering majors at NUS -- the university's own published table directly contradicts that assumption. Never assume NUS's Engineering Scholars or NTU's Renaissance Engineering Programme interview requirement describes ordinary Engineering admission -- both are separate, elite honours sub-tracks. NTU's and SMU's ordinary Engineering mechanisms were not independently verified to NUS's depth this pass.

countries.scope: university (local numero chiuso, using the same TOLC/TOL instrument family as many other high-demand fields)
countries.description: Engineering is not one of Italy's three nationally-restricted numero-chiuso fields (Medicine, Dentistry, Veterinary Medicine, Italian-taught). It runs through the same TOLC/TOL instrument family used broadly across many other Italian fields (Economics, Psychology, Communication, Architecture) -- confirmed directly this pass at Politecnico di Milano for 2026/27: an online entrance test (TOL, or a recognized alternative -- TOLC-I, CEnT-S, or SAT), minimum threshold >=30/100, with candidates ranked (graduatoria) for the capped places, and OFA (the remedial catch-up module) removed for all subjects except English from 2024 onward. This is the identical instrument and binding/non-binding toggle the country doc already documents generally -- Engineering becomes 'restricted' purely through local, university-set capacity limits at competitive institutions, the same local numero-chiuso mechanism popular Economics or Psychology programmes use.
countries.eligibility_determinants: Secondary diploma plus a TOL/TOLC-I/CEnT-S/SAT score; at open programmes the score is non-binding orientation (a low score can trigger the OFA remedial module); at locally capped programmes (e.g. Politecnico di Milano) the score is the binding ranking criterion against a minimum threshold.
countries.strengthens_application: A strong TOL/TOLC-I score, since at capacity-constrained universities it directly determines rank order, not just eligibility.
countries.largely_irrelevant: Personal statements, recommendation letters, extracurricular activity -- absent as Engineering-specific levers, consistent with Italy's general qualification/test-threshold admission model.
countries.never_infer: Never treat Engineering as one of Italy's nationally-restricted numero-chiuso fields -- it is not; its restriction, where it exists, is local and university-set. Never assume the binding/non-binding TOLC toggle is Engineering-specific -- the same toggle applies to any high-demand Italian field depending on that university's own local capacity decision.
sources: docs/research/admissions-systems/italy.md (Standardized tests, Restricted / selective programmes sections)

countries.scope: national formula, university-set weighting (identical mechanism to any other public Grado)
countries.description: Engineering runs through the identical nota de admision / EBAU / Distrito Unico mechanism as any other Spanish public Grado. The only Engineering-relevant lever is Real Decreto 534/2024's subject-weighting bonus -- typically Mathematics II and Physics weighted at 0.2 each for quantitative degrees, applied automatically from the student's best-scoring eligible subjects -- a scoring bonus, not a hard gate or separate instrument, identical in kind to the mechanism used for Medicine or any other public degree. No SAT/ACT/AP role, no dedicated test, no confirmed interview or portfolio for public-university Engineering. Private-university Engineering may run its own separate process, but that reflects Spain's general public/private admissions split, not something Engineering-specific.
countries.eligibility_determinants: Nota de acceso (Bachillerato average plus EBAU) with the automatic weighted-subject bonus applied from Mathematics II/Physics where the target university weights them, compared against that cycle's self-adjusting nota de corte.
countries.strengthens_application: Strong Mathematics II and Physics Bachillerato/EBAU performance specifically, since these are the commonly-weighted subjects for quantitative degrees -- the same lever that strengthens any weighted-subject Spanish application, not unique to Engineering.
countries.largely_irrelevant: SAT/ACT/AP scores, personal statements, interviews -- no confirmed role in public-university Engineering admission.
countries.never_infer: Never assume Spanish public-university Engineering has any separate test, interview, or portfolio layer -- it runs the identical nota de admision/Distrito Unico formula as any other public Grado. Never assume a private university's separate Engineering process reflects an Engineering-specific Spanish pattern rather than the general public/private admissions split.
sources: docs/research/admissions-systems/spain.md (Subject prerequisites, Standardized tests, Restricted / selective programmes sections)

countries.scope: programme-set points/subject minimum within the national CAO points mechanism
countries.description: Engineering is not one of CAO's 'restricted-application course' categories (unlike Medicine, Nursing, or Art & Design) -- it runs through the ordinary Leaving Certificate points system. The national Higher Level Mathematics +25-point bonus applies (not Engineering-exclusive -- it applies to any applicant with HL Maths among their best six subjects), and individual programmes set their own point/subject minimums: UCD's own non-EU table shows 'B3 3rd level' for Engineering against 'C2 3rd level / 4.5 Lise' for Business/Computer Science and 'D1 3rd level / 2 Lise' for Economics/Social Science for the identical Turkish diploma -- real institution-level variation in bar height, using the identical points mechanism throughout. No HPAT-style dedicated aptitude test, no mandatory interview, no portfolio requirement for standard Engineering admission.
countries.eligibility_determinants: Leaving Certificate (or equivalent) points total from best-6-subjects, plus any programme-set minimum subject grade (commonly Mathematics), plus the national HL Maths +25-point bonus where applicable -- the identical CAO points mechanism used for non-restricted courses generally.
countries.strengthens_application: A high Higher Level Mathematics grade specifically, both for the direct points contribution and the national +25-point bonus where it lands among the applicant's best six subjects.
countries.largely_irrelevant: Essays, references, interviews, portfolios -- absent from CAO/points-route Engineering admission exactly as they are absent from the CAO route generally.
countries.never_infer: Never assume Engineering is a CAO 'restricted-application course' -- it is not, unlike Medicine or Art & Design. Never assume one university's programme-specific points/subject minimum (e.g. UCD's non-EU Engineering table) generalizes to another Irish university without checking that university's own current table.

countries.scope: programme (floating ATAR/selection-rank cutoff, plus a general prerequisite/assumed-knowledge mechanism not exclusive to Engineering)
countries.description: Engineering carries none of Medicine's specific structural additions: no Commonwealth Supported Place government place-count exception (CSP funding for Engineering, as for most Australian fields, is allocated to universities in dollars, not a fixed number of places), no UCAT ANZ/ISAT requirement, no mandatory interview. It runs through the same floating ATAR/selection-rank mechanism used for most Australian programmes. Mathematics (and at some universities Physics) is commonly a hard 'prerequisite' -- the country doc's documented, named distinction from softer 'assumed knowledge' -- for Engineering at several universities, but this prerequisite/assumed-knowledge toggle is a general Australian mechanism applied to any mathematics-dependent degree, not unique to Engineering.
countries.eligibility_determinants: ATAR/selection rank meeting that cycle's floating cutoff for the specific programme, plus any programme-set Mathematics (sometimes Physics) prerequisite -- a hard eligibility gate at universities that classify it as a prerequisite, a softer expectation where classified as assumed knowledge only.
countries.strengthens_application: A strong Mathematics (and where relevant Physics) result specifically, both for meeting any hard prerequisite and for competitiveness against the floating ATAR/selection-rank cutoff.
countries.largely_irrelevant: Interviews, portfolios, standardized aptitude tests -- none confirmed as a factor for standard Engineering admission, in contrast to Medicine/Dentistry at the same universities.
countries.never_infer: Never treat 'prerequisite' and 'assumed knowledge' as interchangeable for an Engineering Mathematics requirement -- a subject not meeting a stated prerequisite can make an applicant ineligible outright, while a subject not meeting assumed knowledge typically does not. Never assume Engineering shares Medicine's CSP-place-count government exception -- it is confirmed Medicine-specific.

countries.scope: university (same graduated Rank Score mechanism used broadly; Engineering sits at the top of the published threshold table)
countries.description: Auckland's BE(Hons) Rank Score threshold (250) is the highest published figure in Auckland's own comparison table -- above Nursing's 230 -- but it is the same graduated, continuous, NCEA-credit-based Rank Score mechanism used across most named NZ Bachelor's programmes, not a separate instrument. No confirmed dedicated test, interview, or hard numerical place-cap was found for Engineering this pass, unlike Medicine's confirmed two-stage gateway-then-UCAT-ANZ-plus-MMI model at the same universities. Engineering is 'restricted' here purely in the sense that its Rank Score bar sits at the top of the published table.
countries.eligibility_determinants: University Entrance (national floor) plus a Rank Score meeting the specific programme's published threshold -- the identical graduated NCEA-credit-based mechanism used for most named NZ Bachelor's programmes.
countries.strengthens_application: A high Rank Score built from strong NCEA Achievement Standard credit accumulation, particularly in mathematics/physics-relevant subjects -- the same lever that strengthens any Rank-Score-gated NZ application.
countries.largely_irrelevant: A dedicated aptitude test, interview, or portfolio -- none confirmed for standard Engineering admission, unlike Medicine's UCAT ANZ/MMI or creative-programme portfolio/audition requirements at the same universities.
countries.never_infer: Never assume Engineering follows Medicine's two-stage gateway-then-competitive-progression model at the same NZ universities -- no equivalent second-stage filter was confirmed for Engineering. Never assume Auckland's specific 250 Rank Score threshold applies at other NZ universities without checking that university's own published table.

countries.scope: university (JUPAS merit-order for local applicants; non-JUPAS qualification review for international applicants, confirmed no-interview at HKUST)
countries.description: For local/JUPAS applicants, Engineering is placed by the identical merit-order matching algorithm used for every other JUPAS programme, with Mathematics at Advanced Level commonly required (confirmed for HKUST's STEM-track admission in the country doc). For non-JUPAS/international applicants -- the pathway essentially all Turkish and other internationally-educated applicants use, per RULE-ADMISSIONS-013 -- confirmed directly this pass from HKUST's own School of Engineering FAQ: 'Interview is not a requirement for the School of Engineering... conducted at the discretion of individual programmes' if the university finds it helpful for a specific applicant. This is qualification/transcript review against a published minimum, the same general non-JUPAS mechanism used for most other non-JUPAS fields, and a sharp contrast with this package's own confirmed finding that HKU and CUHK Medicine require a mandatory MMI or panel interview for the identical (non-JUPAS) applicant population.
countries.eligibility_determinants: For JUPAS: Best-5 HKDSE subject scores feeding the merit-order algorithm, with Mathematics at Advanced Level commonly required for STEM programmes. For non-JUPAS: qualification/transcript review against each university's published minimum for the applicant's specific credential type (e.g. IB, A-Level, Turkish diploma).
countries.strengthens_application: For JUPAS, Best-5 score strength directly, since the algorithm is purely merit-order. For non-JUPAS, exceeding the published minimum threshold comfortably, since HKUST states interviews are discretionary rather than a scored, universal component.
countries.largely_irrelevant: Interview preparation specifically for Engineering at HKUST, given its own stated non-requirement -- contrast directly with Medicine at HKU/CUHK, where interview preparation is essential.
countries.never_infer: Never assume Hong Kong Medicine's confirmed mandatory-interview finding (HKU MMI, CUHK panel) extends to Engineering -- HKUST's own FAQ directly contradicts that for its School of Engineering. Never assume a JUPAS applicant and a non-JUPAS applicant face the same Engineering admission mechanism -- they are categorically different pathways, per RULE-ADMISSIONS-013.

countries.scope: national (identical YKS SAY-track placement mechanism as every other SAY-scored programme; restriction is a continuous, cycle-varying cutoff, not a separate category)
countries.description: Engineering is placed entirely by YKS's SAY score type -- the identical (TYT x 0.40) + (AYT x 0.60) + (OBP x 0.12 or 0.06) formula and strict national rank-order placement used for every other SAY-track programme, with no interview, test, or portfolio beyond YKS itself, exactly as the country doc's own explicit statement already establishes ('Medicine, Law, top Engineering programmes remain pure score-ranked placement with no interview or portfolio step at all'). Top programmes require close to the maximum attainable score: illustrative, cycle-specific 2026 figures found this pass put both Bogazici University's and Istanbul Technical University's (ITU) Computer Engineering programmes at roughly 533 points (Bogazici ranked around 1,448th nationally that cycle) -- an extreme cutoff within the same formula, not a different mechanism.
countries.eligibility_determinants: TYT plus AYT Mathematics/Physics/Chemistry/Biology-weighted SAY score, compared in strict national rank order against other candidates who listed the same programme code -- identical in kind to every other SAY-scored lisans programme.
countries.strengthens_application: AYT SAY-cluster subject score maximization -- there is no other lever; leadership, extracurriculars, and essays have zero channel into the domestic placement score, per this package's own established finding for Turkey generally.
countries.largely_irrelevant: Everything that is not a YKS score: essays, recommendations, extracurriculars, interviews, portfolios -- confirmed zero channel for the domestic pathway, matching the country doc's and the sibling counseling-intelligence lane's independently-confirmed finding.
countries.never_infer: Never assume any non-score evidence (leadership, research, competitions) improves a domestic-pathway Turkish Engineering applicant's placement -- zero channel exists for it. Never present a specific cycle's cutoff score/rank (e.g. this pass's ~533-point Bogazici/ITU Computer Engineering figures) as stable across cycles -- re-verify each admissions cycle against OSYM's own results publication.
sources: docs/research/admissions-systems/turkey.md (Subject prerequisites, Standardized tests, Restricted / selective programmes sections)

cross_cutting_patterns: Engineering inverts Medicine's own ratio in this package: Medicine is structurally different in 13 of 15 countries, Engineering in only 5 of 15, with a further 7 numerically-stricter-only and 3 fully same-as-general-admission -- a category Medicine never lands in anywhere in this package. A large, well-funded, high-enrollment field without Medicine's clinical-capacity or licensure-body logic rarely accumulates a dedicated selection apparatus, even where it is highly competitive by cutoff/ATAR/Rank-Score alone.

Where Engineering IS structurally different, the additions cluster into two distinct kinds that should be modeled separately, not merged into one 'has extra requirements' flag: (a) a dedicated admissions-TEST layer shared across a consortium of universities (the UK's ESAT; Germany's TUM-specific Eignungsfeststellungsverfahren, which is file-review-plus-written-statement rather than a timed test), and (b) a separate APPLICATION/DECISION layer -- applying to a named sub-unit with its own essays or a jury outside the general admissions office -- found independently in the US (school-within-university), Canada (Waterloo AIF, U of T OSP-plus-video), and France (concours networks). The 'school-within-university' shape recurring independently in both the US (holistic-review system) and Canada (transcript-driven system) suggests this pattern is tied to how a country's higher-education institutions organize themselves internally (faculties/colleges with devolved admissions authority) rather than to the country's general admissions philosophy -- a candidate cross-cutting pattern distinct from anything already in RULE-ADMISSIONS-001 through 017.

A field can be simultaneously 'restricted' (in the sense of a high, competitive cutoff) and mechanistically identical to general admission -- confirmed cleanly for Turkey, Spain, Ireland, Australia, New Zealand, Hong Kong, and Italy's Engineering. ORYN must not treat 'this programme is hard to get into' as evidence of a different admissions mechanism; the two are independent facts, and this package's Engineering research is the clearest full-package illustration of that independence found so far.

The same country can hold both a genuinely dual-pathway field (France's Engineering: CPGE-then-concours vs. direct post-bac entry, two temporally and organizationally distinct routes to one credential) and, elsewhere in this same package, a single-pathway field for the identical country -- dual-pathway-ness is a programme-family property, not a country property, and must be checked per family rather than assumed to recur once found for one field in a country.

An elite/honours sub-track within a field can carry a structurally different mechanism (test or interview) even where the ordinary version of that same field is confirmed same-as-general-admission -- found independently at NUS (Engineering Scholars/Engineering and Medicine Track) and NTU (Renaissance Engineering Programme) within Singapore's Engineering research specifically. A 'does Engineering require an interview' question must first resolve whether the student means the ordinary major or a named honours/scholars sub-programme -- these are different questions with different answers at the same university.
unresolved_questions: France: whether a DAP-track (foreign-diploma, non-French/European-Bac) applicant -- the pathway a Turkey-resident MEB-only applicant would generally use per the existing country doc -- can access either Geipi Polytech or Puissance Alpha at all was not confirmed either way this pass; both networks' public materials describe French/European-Bac eligibility without an explicit DAP-track statement.

Germany: whether TUM's Eignungsfeststellungsverfahren pattern generalizes to other German technical universities beyond TUM and (in its absence) RWTH Aachen was not exhaustively checked -- a genuine gap, not a confirmed two-university-only finding; whether RWTH Aachen's other engineering fields (Elektrotechnik, Bauingenieurwesen) share Maschinenbau's currently-zulassungsfrei status was not independently verified.

United States: the school-within-university pattern was confirmed at three universities on two platforms; its prevalence against the 'roughly half of top-100 universities' figure the country doc already cites for capacity-constrained CS/engineering majors was not re-derived or exhaustively mapped this pass.
Canada: whether any major Canadian university beyond Waterloo, University of Toronto, and UBC uses an Engineering-specific supplementary-application layer was not checked.

Singapore: NTU's and SMU's ordinary (non-honours) Engineering admission mechanisms were confirmed only at the level of 'no general interview found,' not researched to NUS's field-by-field table depth; SMU's Engineering-adjacent programmes were not separately checked at all this pass.

Switzerland: whether EPFL's own single-tier entrance examination for Engineering differs in any Engineering-specific way from its treatment of other fields was not independently re-verified this pass, beyond the general finding already in the country doc that EPFL's mechanism is field-agnostic.

Turkey: the illustrative ~533-point cutoff figures for Bogazici/ITU Computer Engineering came from secondary aggregator sources (kariyer.net), not OSYM's own primary results publication, and should be re-verified against a primary source before being presented to a student as authoritative.

Netherlands: the full national list of which specific Engineering-adjacent programmes (beyond TU Delft's CSE and Aerospace Engineering) carry numerus fixus at other Dutch technical universities (Eindhoven, Twente) was not exhaustively mapped this pass.
